title: Satta and Balvand
hook: two minstrels who, tradition says, quarreled with Guru Arjan and were forgiven; their Var is in the Granth (Ramkali, ang 966–968)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bhatts, poets of praise, who sang the Gurus as one light. Today, two musicians who walked out.

Two musicians, a rebab and a voice, singing kirtan in the Guru's court: Satta and Balvand. Then, tradition says, something goes wrong. A request for money, a quarrel, wounded pride. They stop singing, say hard things about the house they served, and walk out. A falling-out could end right there. This one ends with their song inside the Guru Granth Sahib, in Raag Ramkali, Ang 966, kept and sung beside the Gurus' own words.
screen: `TWO MUSICIANS IN THE GURU'S COURT.` → `A QUARREL, AND A WALKOUT.` → `THEIR SONG IN THE GRANTH.`

segments.voice: First the story, as tradition tells it. Satta and Balvand ask Guru Arjan for help, and when it isn't what they hoped, pride takes over. They refuse to play, and boast that the Gurus' fame rests on their music. Without the court, their fortunes sink. In the end they come back humbled, asking forgiveness, and tradition says a devoted Sikh pleaded for them. The Guru forgives them, and they pick up the rebab again. Now the text, which is what the Granth actually keeps: their Var, a ballad, in Raag Ramkali. It doesn't sing about themselves. It sings about Guru Nanak setting up Lehna as the next Guru, Guru Angad, and the line passing on. One of its lines, in paraphrase: the light is the same, the way is the same; the master has only changed the body. It's the claim the Bhatts made yesterday, but listen to who's making it now. Two men who once claimed the Gurus needed them end up singing that the Guru is one light, needing nothing from anyone, passing from body to body. The quarrel was about who mattered. The song answers it: the light matters, and everyone else is a singer. And notice what the Guru did. He didn't just let them back in the door. Their words went into the scripture, sung in gurdwaras alongside his own. Forgiveness here isn't a grudging truce. It's a microphone handed back.
screen: `A REQUEST, A QUARREL, A WALKOUT.` · `HUMBLED, THEY COME BACK; THE GURU FORGIVES.` · `THE SAME LIGHT, ONLY THE BODY CHANGED.` · `A MICROPHONE HANDED BACK.` · then, large: `FORGIVEN, AND SUNG.`

segments.voice: Choose a small quarrel, sized for two minutes: a sharp exchange, a slight, a door that closed, and let the other person's face come to mind. You don't have to call them or pretend it didn't happen; just loosen your grip on it, one breath at a time, and if something in you is ready, imagine handing them their voice back. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.
Var. A ballad: Satta and Balvand's, in Raag Ramkali, singing that the light is the same, the way is the same, only the body has changed.
Your line: forgiven, and sung. The walkout wasn't the end of their story. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Var of Satta and Balvand in Raag Ramkali is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs tell their story as one of pride, return and forgiveness.

chat.says: Satta and Balvand walked out on the Guru. Why is their song in the scripture?
options: Tradition says they came back humbled, the Guru forgave them, and their Var was kept.
They paid the court to add it, as the price of being let back in.

chat.meaning: Tradition says the Guru forgave the returning minstrels; their Var in Raag Ramkali sings that the light is the same and only the body changed.

rebab.meaning: a stringed instrument played in kirtan

Ramkali.meaning: the raag, or musical mode, of their Var

Lehna.meaning: Guru Angad's name before he became Guru

notes: The quarrel story (request for help, refusal to play, boasting, decline, return, intercession by a devoted Sikh, traditionally Bhai Ladha of Lahore) is attributed to tradition; the intercessor is left unnamed. Confirm.
Paraphrase of 'joti ohaa jugat saai sahi kaaiaa pher palateeai': confirm wording and 'one of its best-known lines' (softer phrasing may be preferred).
The Var's subject (Guru Nanak installing Lehna as Guru Angad, and the succession) is summarized; the Var also praises later Gurus. Confirm.
'Sung in gurdwaras alongside his own' is general; confirm.
Index places Satta and Balvand under 'the other Bhagats'; they are minstrels (rababis), not Bhagats, which the script reflects.
